sources.publisher: Georgia State University, Department of Physics and Astronomy (HyperPhysics)
sources.title: Conductors and Insulators
sources.authorityRationale: HyperPhysics is authored by Carl R. Nave, Professor Emeritus of Physics, and is hosted directly on Georgia State University's own physics department server -- a genuine academic-institution publication, not a third-party mirror.

supports.claimSummary: In a conductor, outer electrons are loosely bound and free to move, so charge moves relatively readily (comparatively low resistance/resistivity).

In an insulator, even the outermost electrons are tightly bound, so charge movement is strongly opposed (negligible/extremely small current at ordinary voltages); resistivity is very large (example: glass ~10^12 ohm-m vs copper ~1.7x10^-8 ohm-m).
Electron mobility (loosely bound outer electrons free to move through the material) is what allows a conductor to carry current.

sources.publisher: Georgia State University, Department of Physics and Astronomy (HyperPhysics)
sources.title: Resistance and Resistivity
sources.authorityRationale: HyperPhysics, hosted directly on Georgia State University's physics department server.

supports.claimSummary: Resistance is the ratio of the voltage applied to a component to the current which flows through it.
Resistivity is the factor in resistance that accounts for the nature of the material, used with geometry to calculate the resistance of a wire; unit ohm-metre; symbol rho.
R = rho*L/A, with R=resistance (ohms), rho=resistivity of the material, L=length, A=cross-sectional area.
Resistance definition R = V/I is itself one rearrangement of V=IR.

sources.publisher: Georgia State University, Department of Physics and Astronomy (HyperPhysics)
sources.title: Electric current
sources.authorityRationale: HyperPhysics, hosted directly on Georgia State University's physics department server.

supports.claimSummary: Electric current is the rate of charge flow past a point in a circuit (I = charge/time), measured in coulombs/second = amperes (1A = 1C/s).

Although electrons are the actual charge carriers in conductors, convention takes the direction of current as if positive charges were moving (high to low voltage); this is opposite the true electron-drift direction, though both give identical results for circuit analysis.

sources.title: Ohm's Law
sources.authorityRationale: HyperPhysics, hosted directly on Georgia State University's physics department server.

supports.claimSummary: For many conductors, current is directly proportional to applied voltage; the voltage/current ratio (resistance) is constant over a wide range of voltages only for 'ohmic' materials -- Ohm's law is conditional, not universal.
Amperes = volts/ohms (I=V/R), rearranged to the standard form V=IR, with V=voltage, I=current, R=resistance.

supports.claimSummary: Power = Voltage x Current (P=VI); power dissipated in a resistor depends on the square of the current, so high-voltage/low-current distribution minimises loss.

supports.claimSummary: The electric field inside a resistor equals the voltage drop across the resistor divided by its length; this voltage drop is the potential difference that appears across a resistance carrying current.
The page derives, from the voltage drop across a resistor and the resulting current, the standard relationship V = IR (its equation 12).

sources.title: IET Wiring Matters: 'How voltage drop can affect EV charging point open PEN detection devices' (July 2023, issue 96)
sources.authorityRationale: The IET is the UK's chartered professional body for engineering and technology and the publisher of BS 7671 (IET Wiring Regulations); this is its own free-access technical magazine, hosted on its own domain.

supports.claimSummary: Voltage drop = (mV/A/m) x Ib x Length / 1000, where mV/A/m is the cable's tabulated voltage-drop factor, Ib is the design current and Length is the circuit length. BS 7671 Table 4Ab's 5% figure (for a load other than lighting, supplied directly from a public low-voltage distribution system) is a recommended, informative value for that specific context, not a universal permitted maximum -- the acceptable voltage drop in a real design depends on the connected equipment's requirements.

supports.claimSummary: Power dissipated (Joule heating) = P = I^2R = IV.
P = I^2R = IV (confirms P=VI from a second source).
The power dissipated in a resistor as heat (Joule heating) is P=I^2R=IV -- the thermal effect of current.
Resistors in series: Req = R1 + R2 + ...
Resistors in parallel: Req^-1 = R1^-1 + R2^-1 + ...
Microscopic derivation: conductivity sigma=ne^2*tau/m, resistivity rho=1/sigma, giving R = rho*L/A.

sources.publisher: East Tennessee State University, Department of Physics and Astronomy
sources.title: PHYS-2020: General Physics II, Course Lecture Notes, Section IV (Direct Current Circuits), Edition 4.0
sources.authorityRationale: Hosted directly on East Tennessee State University's own faculty server, authored by Dr. Donald G. Luttermoser, ETSU, as the department's own course lecture notes.
sources.locator: ETSU PHYS-2020 Section IV, pp. IV-2 to IV-7 (resistors in series/parallel; example IV-1 on DC circuit power)

supports.claimSummary: The current through all resistors in a series circuit is the same: I = I1 = I2 = ... (Eq. IV-3).
Req = R1+R2 (Eq. IV-4), generalised to Req = sum(Ri) for N series resistors (Eq. IV-5).
For series resistors, deltaV = deltaV1+deltaV2 = I1*R1+I2*R2 = I*R1+I*R2 -- the supply voltage is shared among the resistors and the individual voltage drops sum to it.
When resistors are connected in parallel, the potential difference across them is the same: deltaV = deltaV1 = deltaV2 (Eq. IV-6).
The current entering a parallel circuit equals the sum of the currents through each branch: I = I1+I2 (Eq. IV-7).
1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 (Eq. IV-8), generalised to 1/Req = sum(1/Ri) for N parallel resistors (Eq. IV-9).

Worked example IV-1: given total power P and equivalent resistance Req, P = (deltaV)^2/Req, so deltaV = sqrt(P*Req). P=V^2/R itself is unconditional for a resistor given the actual voltage across it; the example's negligible-internal-resistance assumption instead applies to substituting the source's emf E in place of the actual load voltage deltaV.

Worked example IV-1 demonstrates a full DC-circuit power-calculation procedure: reduce a series/parallel resistor network step-by-step to a single equivalent resistance, then use P=(deltaV)^2/Req to find the unknown emf/voltage from the given power.
